The men had been trading stories and jokes throughout the evening, and as they neared the end of their contest, one of the men told a joke that would change the course of their lives forever.

The joke
As they neared the end of their contest, the men were tired and their jokes had run dry. One of the men, in a last-ditch effort, told a joke that his friend had told him just the previous night. He said, "You know what I think about that? I think it's a load of bull!" His friend, who had been saving his jokes for the contest, was stumped. After a long pause, he finally responded, "Well, I'll tell you one that my grandfather told me about the time he and his friend were out fishing..." The first man interrupted him, "What's it about? That's the same joke my grandfather told me!" The two men laughed, and the contest was over.

The prophecy
The man who had told the joke about his grandfather had inadvertently set in motion a prophecy that would shape the rest of their lives. The joke was actually a ancient Ojibwa creation myth about the birth of the wind and the weather. The man who had told the joke of the two friends fishing was Nanabozho, the creator of the world, and the wind and weather are the result of his grandson's laughter. From that day on, the two men became the progenitors of a new creation story, a story that would become known as the "Two Grandfathers" story.

They drifted far out to sea, and after many days they were rescued by a passing fishing boat and brought to the village of Kupa'a on the south shore of the river. They told how they had gone down to the river to hunt seals, had been overturned by the storm, and had been rescued by a fishing boat. One night two men from Egulac went down to the river for a swim. They were Egush and Eylak, friends since childhood. They swam and they talked and they swam some more. The sun had set and the moon had risen and they were still in the water. Suddenly a noise like a gunshot rang out. They looked up and saw that the moon had fallen out of the sky and was coming their way. They swam to the bank and looked around. There was no sign of the moon on the water, but they could see the reflection of the full moon on the opposite bank. They were facing south, and behind them to the north was the dark shape of the mountain.
They were afraid and didn't know what to do. They couldn't swim back across the river in the dark. They couldn't go around the mountain to the north, and they couldn't go up the mountain to the west. The only other possibility was to go east through the forest. They could see the trees as dark shapes against the moonlit sky. They could hear the animals moving in the forest. They were scared, and they decided to go back to the safety of their village. They swam back across the river, and they were out of the water and running through the forest before the moon fell out of the sky for the second time. They were shaking and sweating as they ran. They didn't look back. They didn't stop running until they were safely hidden in the bushes just outside their village.
They were wet and cold, and they were shaking from their head to their feet. They had left their clothes behind in their haste to escape. They huddled together under a tree, and they began to shiver uncontrollably. They were naked and afraid, and they didn't know what had caused the moon to fall from the sky. They only knew that they were in danger and that they needed to find a way to get back to the safety of their village

Their bodies were carried up the river and they were buried in the place where the river came together and formed a lake. The people of Egulac were very sad. They missed their two young men. They searched for them along the river and along the lake. They looked for them day and night. They were sad and worried. Finally after many days they found them. They pulled them out of the water and took them home. They were happy to have their two young men back. They were happy to have their heroes back. They were heroes because they had fought the flood and swam across the river during the flood to get to higher ground. They were heroes because they saved the people of Egulac from the flood.
